title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
AI tools were used to generate fake videos and social media profiles impersonating a real, named immigration attorney. The fabricated content presented him as offering services he never provided, and it spread across TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram at scale before being detected. The failure here is impersonation: AI-generated synthetic media used to deceive people into believing they were dealing with a legitimate professional.

The deployment point where this happened was public social media, not inside any single product or institution. Detection came only after victims began contacting the real attorney's office, meaning no platform-level check caught the fake profiles before they caused harm. The volume, nearly 6,500 profiles requiring removal by a third-party anti-piracy firm, indicates the content replicated faster than any manual review process was able to intercept it.

What is not established is who the scammers are, whether any platform was aware of the fraud before the attorney's intervention, or whether any victim has received restitution. The reported financial loss by at least one victim is described in news coverage, not confirmed by any legal or regulatory finding.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become a victim of identity theft involving artificial intelligence. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using AI-generated images and videos that depict Leal offering immigration services he never provided. The scammers use these videos to target vulnerable immigrants, offering services like US residency assistance for $2,200 in cash. Leal discovered the fraud when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity first appeared last October and has dramatically escalated in recent months.

To combat the scheme, Leal hired an online anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The scams typically start with social media videos directing victims to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters exchange phony contracts and request payment through money transfer apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams and is warning immigrants to verify anyone offering legal services online and avoid paying for immigration services through informal payment methods.
